solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: Fruit spread and fruit jam (9,6)

blocks.note: butter is a spread for bread
the second 'fruit': a nut is botanically a fruit
to jam = to squash, cram together

annotation.surface: A breakfast table with fruit spread and fruit jam on offer.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Fruit spread' and 'fruit jam' read as two preserves; the pieces are actually 'spread', 'fruit' and 'jam', each standing alone, with the first 'Fruit' as the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: A butternut squash is botanically a fruit, since it carries the plant's seeds.

entries.clue: Rustic family under awful pressure (7)

indicators.note: in a down clue, KIN sits below BUM+P

blocks.note: bum = bad, awful (British slang, as in 'a bum deal')

annotation.surface: A country family crushed under terrible pressure.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Rustic' looks like an adjective describing the family; it is the definition, used as a noun for a country yokel.
annotation.definitionFit: A rustic is an unsophisticated country person, which is exactly a bumpkin.

entries.clue: Weary and embarrassed after sex on the rebound (5)

indicators.note: bouncing back turns IT round to TI
after in the sense of later in the sequence, so RED is written behind TI

annotation.surface: Someone worn out and red-faced after a fling with an ex, on the rebound.
annotation.walkthrough: 'On the rebound' reads as romance after a break-up; here it just turns IT backwards.
annotation.definitionFit: Weary and tired both mean lacking energy.

entries.clue: Height of joy, taking possession of electric vehicle (9)

indicators.note: ELATION takes EV inside it

blocks.note: EV is the standard abbreviation for electric vehicle

annotation.surface: The peak of happiness: finally getting the keys to an electric car.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Height of joy' reads as one phrase; 'Height' is the definition and 'of' only links it to the wordplay.
annotation.definitionFit: Elevation is height above a level, such as sea level.

entries.clue: Not one satisfactory corner (4)

blocks.note: no = not one, as in 'no seats left'

annotation.surface: A complaint that not a single corner is acceptable.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Not one satisfactory' reads as a single verdict on the corners, but it breaks after 'one': 'no' can mean 'not one', as in 'no seats left'.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a nook is a small sheltered recess, like a corner by the fire.

entries.clue: Regularly target a certain prize (8)

indicators.note: take every other letter: T, R, E of TaRgEt

blocks.note: first, third and fifth letters of TARGET

annotation.surface: Advice to keep aiming at one particular prize.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Prize' looks like a noun, the thing being targeted; it is the verb, to value highly.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, both verbs: you treasure what you value highly, as you prize it.

entries.clue: Ring you and cry after Question Time (5)

indicators.note: after in the sense of following in order, so U and OI are written behind the Q

blocks.note: U = you, as in text messages
oi! is a cry to get attention

annotation.surface: A plea to phone someone and weep once Question Time, the BBC political debate show, is over.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Ring' looks like a verb, to phone; it is the noun. Question Time is a long-running BBC panel show, but here the two words just give Q and T.
annotation.definitionFit: A quoit is a ring thrown over a peg in the game of quoits.

entries.clue: Loathsome earthborn mutant (9)

indicators.note: a mutant is an altered form, so the letters change

annotation.surface: A horror-film creature: a disgusting mutant born of the earth.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Mutant' sits at the end like a noun completing the monster; its sense of changed form is what scrambles EARTHBORN.
annotation.definitionFit: Abhorrent means inspiring disgust, as loathsome does.

entries.clue: Vacuous hippy breeds furry animals (7)

indicators.note: empty, so HIPPY loses its inside letters, leaving H and Y

annotation.surface: An empty-headed hippy keeps breeding fluffy pets.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Breeds' reads as a verb for what the hippy does; it is the noun, meaning races. A hyrax is a small furry African mammal.
annotation.definitionFit: Hyraxes (plural also hyraces) are small furry African mammals that look like guinea pigs.

entries.clue: Communication system originally mixing ogham, runes and minute lines (5,4)

indicators.note: take the first letter of each of the next three words

blocks.note: first letters of Mixing, Ogham, Runes
a minute and a sec are both a short moment: 'wait a sec'
an ode is some lines of verse

annotation.surface: A history of writing that began by blending ogham, runes and tiny marks.
annotation.walkthrough: Ogham and runes are ancient scripts and 'minute lines' suggests dots and dashes, so the surface pulls towards the answer; 'minute' is the noun, a moment, not the adjective meaning tiny.
annotation.definitionFit: Morse code is a system for sending messages by dots and dashes.

entries.clue: One of two parents shedding clothes (5)

indicators.note: the outer letters are the word's clothing, so MOTHERS loses M and S

blocks.note: MOTHERS without its first and last letters

annotation.surface: One parent in a couple getting undressed.
annotation.walkthrough: 'One of two' reads as part of the surface, one of a pair of parents; it is the definition, as in 'one or the other'.
annotation.definitionFit: With a pair, 'the other' is the second one of two.

entries.clue: Guy with racing tip in Shanghai? (6)

blocks.note: to guy someone is to make fun of them; so is to kid
a nap is a tipster's single most confident tip of the day in British horse racing

annotation.surface: A man in Shanghai with a hot tip for the races.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Guy' looks like a man and 'Shanghai' like the city; they are both verbs. To shanghai is to force someone aboard a ship, hence the question mark.
annotation.definitionFit: To shanghai is to abduct someone, originally to crew a ship, which is to kidnap them.

entries.clue: Obscure English boozer west of Clapton? (8)

indicators.note: in an across answer, west is to the left, so E+SOT comes before ERIC

blocks.note: Eric Clapton, the guitarist; the ? marks a first name clued by example

annotation.surface: An odd English pub in west London, near Clapton.
annotation.walkthrough: In Britain a boozer is also a pub, and Clapton is an area of London, so the surface is a pub west of Clapton; the boozer here is a drunk.
annotation.definitionFit: Esoteric means understood only by a few, which is obscure.

entries.clue: Author beginning to talk playwright round (6)

indicators.note: take the first letter of TALK
brought round, as in turned to face the other way, so T+IBSEN is read backwards

blocks.note: Henrik Ibsen, the Norwegian playwright, placed after the T before the whole is turned round

annotation.surface: A writer starting to win a dramatist over in conversation.
annotation.walkthrough: E. Nesbit wrote The Railway Children, a classic of British children's fiction.
annotation.definitionFit: Edith Nesbit was an English author of children's books.

entries.clue: Drinks with leading baseball player (9)

blocks.note: shorts are small measures of spirits

annotation.surface: Out for drinks with a star baseball player.
annotation.walkthrough: In Britain a short is a spirit served in a small measure, as against a long drink.
annotation.definitionFit: The shortstop is the fielder between second and third base.

entries.clue: Lack of moisture in canned sardines (8)

indicators.note: canned is slang for drunk, so the letters are in disorder

annotation.surface: A complaint that tinned sardines are too dry.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Canned' reads as tinned fish; it is slang for drunk.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: arid describes land with too little water, and -ness makes it the noun for that state.

entries.clue: Unknown quantity of concealed heroin (4,5)

annotation.surface: An uncertain amount of heroin hidden away.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Unknown quantity' reads as an amount of drugs; it is a phrase for a person nobody can predict.
annotation.definitionFit: A dark horse is someone whose abilities are unknown, an unknown quantity.

entries.clue: Coffee sample from cafe’s press officer (8)

indicators.note: a sample is a piece taken out of the words that follow

annotation.surface: A café's PR officer handing out coffee to taste.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Sample' fits the coffee tasting so well that it reads as the café's own offer; it is the instruction to take letters from inside the phrase.
annotation.definitionFit: Espresso is strong coffee made by forcing steam through the grounds.

entries.clue: Like a fool, Nemo perhaps loses faith at first (8)

indicators.note: Nemo is one example of a clownfish
what is lost is no longer there, so the letter is removed from CLOWNFISH
the letter to go is F, the first of FAITH

blocks.note: Nemo in Finding Nemo is a clownfish

annotation.surface: Nemo acting the fool after losing his faith.
annotation.walkthrough: Nemo is the clownfish hero of the Pixar film Finding Nemo; 'faith' has nothing to do with belief, it just supplies its first letter.
annotation.definitionFit: Clownish means behaving like a clown, a fool.

entries.clue: Each university fellow introduces something going over one’s head (7)

indicators.note: CHAP comes first and leads into EA+U

blocks.note: ea. is the abbreviation for each

annotation.surface: Each university fellow opening with a lecture that is beyond the audience.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Going over one's head' suggests something too hard to follow; taken literally it is a hat.
annotation.definitionFit: A chapeau is a hat, which goes over one's head.

entries.clue: Lying around in bedsit, arguing for nothing (6)

indicators.note: the answer lies in the words
turned around, so the hidden letters are read from right to left
it is inside BEDSIT, ARGUING

blocks.note: bedSIT ARGuing, read backwards to give the answer

annotation.surface: Lounging in a bedsit, picking a fight over nothing.
annotation.walkthrough: A bedsit is a British one-room rental flat. 'For nothing' reads as a pointless argument; it means free of charge.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym borrowed from Latin, where gratis means 'as a favour', hence without payment.

entries.clue: Spot policemen cycling on Greece’s borders (7)

indicators.note: the last letter of PLODS goes round to the front
a country's borders are its edges, so only the first and last letters of GREECE are kept
in a down clue, SPLOD sits on top of GE

blocks.note: PLODS with the S moved to the front
first and last letters of GREECE

annotation.surface: Spotting police on bicycles near the Greek frontier.
annotation.walkthrough: Plod is British slang for the police, after Mr Plod the policeman in the Noddy books. 'Spot' reads as a verb, to see; it is the noun, a blot.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, mostly British and informal: a splodge is an irregular spot of ink, paint or colour.

entries.clue: Writer probing another badly flawed protagonist (8)

indicators.note: I pokes into the jumbled letters
ANOTHER is written badly, jumbled

blocks.note: the writer of the clue is I, the setter

annotation.surface: A writer digging into another's poorly drawn main character.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Badly' seems to describe 'flawed'; it only jumbles ANOTHER.
annotation.definitionFit: An antihero is a central character without the usual heroic virtues.

entries.clue: How do you do Shakespeare play without leading pair? (5)

indicators.note: drop the first two letters

annotation.surface: A question about how to stage a Shakespeare play missing its two leads.
annotation.walkthrough: 'How do you do' reads as a practical question; it is the greeting.
annotation.definitionFit: 'How do you do' is a formal greeting, like hello.

entries.clue: Tremble after one becomes a slave (6)

indicators.note: the I that comes after the H
to become is to turn into something else, so the I turns into A

annotation.surface: Someone shaking once they are made a slave.
annotation.walkthrough: 'A slave' reads as one phrase; the 'a' belongs to the wordplay, as the letter replacing I.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym from Old Norse; a thrall was a bondservant, the sense kept alive in 'enthralled'.

entries.clue: Fighter pilot knocked back British bitter (5)

indicators.note: something knocked back is driven backwards, so BR is written back to front

blocks.note: an ace is a top fighter pilot

annotation.surface: A fighter pilot drinking a pint of British bitter.
annotation.walkthrough: Bitter is a British beer, and 'knocked back' suggests drinking it; here bitter is the adjective and knocked back reverses BR.
annotation.definitionFit: Acerb means sour or bitter in taste or temper.

entries.clue: Reportedly shot seabird (4)

indicators.note: a report is something told out loud, so what follows is judged by its sound

blocks.note: a shot = a turn, a go

annotation.surface: A news item: a seabird has been shot.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Shot' reads as a gunshot; it is a go, as in 'have a shot'.
annotation.definitionFit: A tern is a slender seabird related to the gull.

entries.clue: Praise tax cut on back of The Times (5)

indicators.note: the back of a word is its end, so this takes the last letter of THE
placed on, in the sense of added on after, so TOL follows E+X
TOLL loses its last letter

blocks.note: x is the multiplication sign, times
TOLL, a tax, with the last letter cut

annotation.surface: Applauding a tax cut printed on the back page of The Times.
annotation.walkthrough: 'The Times' looks like the newspaper this crossword appears in; it splits into E and X.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym; extol is the more formal verb, from Latin for 'raise up', so it means praise lavishly.

entries.clue: Vanguard at this point moved fast, according to Spooner (9)

indicators.note: swap the opening sounds of the two words, as Rev. Spooner did

blocks.note: moved fast = sped; it hands its opening SP over and takes an H in exchange
at this point = here; it gives up its H and takes the SP back

annotation.surface: An army's front line rushing forward at this point.
annotation.walkthrough: The Rev. William Spooner, an Oxford don, was known for swapping the starts of words, so the clue's pair is said with its opening sounds exchanged.
annotation.definitionFit: The spearhead is the leading force of an attack, the vanguard.

entries.clue: Non-European club playing? Impossible to say (15)

indicators.note: the letters are played about with

annotation.surface: A football club from outside Europe whose name no one can pronounce.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Impossible to say' reads as a shrug about the match; it is the definition, meaning unsayable.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain gloss: the suffix -able means 'can be', so un- and -able together give 'cannot be pronounced'.
